articles.title: Apple’s Siri AI Roadmap: Ternus Details Future Plans
articles.excerpt: The Earnings‑Call Reveal: What John Ternus Said During Apple’s most recent quarterly earnings call, CEO John Ternus fielded a barrage of questions about Siri’s artificial‑intelligence capabilities. Th…
articles.body: The Earnings‑Call Reveal: What John Ternus Said During Apple’s most recent quarterly earnings call, CEO John Ternus fielded a barrage of questions about Siri’s artificial‑intelligence capabilities. The core message was clear: the Siri that ships today is only the first iteration of a much larger vision. Ternus described Siri AI as “primarily request‑based today” but emphasized that Apple has built it on a “modern, orchestrator‑driven architecture” that leaves ample room for expansion. Key takeaways from the call: Request‑based foundation – Siri still relies on explicit user prompts, but the underlying platform is designed for richer interactions.

articles.title: Routing inbound CV e-mails to the right job opening, without an LLM
articles.excerpt: I build HRSpeeder, an applicant tracking system (ATS) for small companies. This post The problem Small companies still receive most applications by e-mail. A candidate writes "Application – Warehouse…
articles.body: I build HRSpeeder , an applicant tracking system (ATS) for small companies. This post describes how our inbound e-mail routing works in production today, including what we deliberately left out. The problem Small companies still receive most applications by e-mail. A candidate writes "Application – Warehouse operator", attaches a PDF, and sends it to a generic address. The recruiter then has to: save the CV somewhere, figure out which job it is for, create a record in a spreadsheet or an ATS. At 2 minutes per e-mail, 200 applications for one job means more than 6 hours of pure data entry, before reading a single CV. We wanted that number to be zero, without asking candidates to use a form. The pipeline Every organization gets a receiving address ( apply+<tag>@inbox.hrspeeder.com ).

articles.title: I Forked an Open-Source Mac Utility. Here's What I Changed, What I Kept, and When You Should Use the Original
articles.excerpt: Most AI coding tools now meter you in windows. A five-hour session here, a weekly cap there, a monthly billing cycle somewhere else, and every provider shows it on a different page. When you use more…
articles.body: Most AI coding tools now meter you in windows. A five-hour session here, a weekly cap there, a monthly billing cycle somewhere else, and every provider shows it on a different page. When you use more than one of them, "how much do I have left before this resets?" turns into three browser tabs and a guess. That question is how I ended up forking an open-source Mac app and selling the result. Since that combination makes people suspicious (fairly), this post is the full picture: what the original does, what I changed, what I kept, and who should skip my version entirely. The original: CodexBar CodexBar is a macOS 14+ menu bar app by Peter Steinberger, released under the MIT license. Its tagline is "Every AI coding limit, in your menu bar," and it delivers on that.

articles.title: Start and end a voice agent call in Python without clipping a word
articles.excerpt: Every phone call has two fragile boundaries: the pickup and the hang-up. In real-time voice agents, these edges are where conversations lose words. A caller starts speaking the millisecond they hear t…
articles.body: Every phone call has two fragile boundaries: the pickup and the hang-up. In real-time voice agents, these edges are where conversations lose words. A caller starts speaking the millisecond they hear the line connect, often well before your client application has finished handshaking with the upstream speech API. Minutes later, as the conversation wraps up, the agent begins saying goodbye, only for the client to assume the exchange is over and abruptly sever the socket mid-sentence. To see how words get lost at the edges, look at this scripted call from the companion repository, pmckeetx/barge-in-voice-agent , connecting to PolyAI's Dialog-RSN-1 API.

articles.title: Stop your voice agent going quiet after it refunds a caller
articles.excerpt: A caller rings a kitchen shop about a cast iron skillet that arrived cracked, hoping to get their money back. The voice agent politely replies, "Let me process that refund for you now." While the paym…
articles.body: A caller rings a kitchen shop about a cast iron skillet that arrived cracked, hoping to get their money back. The voice agent politely replies, "Let me process that refund for you now." While the payment provider processes the transaction in the background, everyday life intervenes: the caller murmurs a quiet "mm-hmm," the evening news buzzes on a nearby television, or the caller suddenly remembers something and shouts, "Wait, wrong card!" Real-time voice agents inhabit a messy world of background noise and spontaneous interruptions. When I set out to test these scenarios, I wanted to answer two practical questions: Which of these everyday sounds might trick an agent into issuing a duplicate refund?

articles.title: This supernova impostor baffled astronomers for 15 years — until they found a hidden black hole feeding on an unstable star
articles.excerpt: A hidden black hole or neutron star companion to an unstable massive star is causing the system to erupt in light that mimics a supernova explosion.
articles.body: A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered. When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 12, 2014: European Philae probe lands on Comet 67P, bounced twice and then got lost for nearly 2 years
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P, then bounced twice and got lost. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P . To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement. The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired. When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space . The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down. Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it . Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.
